To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
untreated high blood pressure is a risk factor for renal damage.
untreated high BP is associated with renal damage at initial diagnosis of HTN.
the subjects diagnosed with stage I or II hypertension showed evidence of sub-clinical renal damage along with the presence proteinuria at the initial diagnosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of untreated hypertension on renal functions at initial diagnosis of HTN.
the early identification of renal dysfunction in patients with hypertension and to emphasize the importance of screening for renal function in hypertensive patients.
the early detection of subclinical renal dysfunction in patients with hypertension, and its correlation with the stages of hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
untreated high blood pressure has a deleterious effect on the renal function tests at the time of initial diagnosis.
untreated high blood pressure at the time of its diagnosis has an impact on renal function tests, which can be used as an early marker of organ damage.
, the renal function tests were found to be on higher normal side and proteinuria was more in hypertensive stages-I and II as compared to pre hypertensive stage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
early detection and treatment of hypertension is necessary to avoid renal damage.
early detection of HTN, and aggressive treatment to achieve BP goals would be beneficial in delaying the progression of renal damage.
early diagnosis, treatment and follow up is necessary in hypertensive population, as early intervention may prevent or delay renal damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
early identification and aggressive management of hypertension can prevent renal damage.
, early diagnosis and treatment of hypertension is important to prevent end organ damage.
early detection of high BP is important to prevent the development of target organ damage and to reduce the morbidity and mortality of hypertension.
